title: HDFC Bank CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan to Step Down After Three Decades
excerpt: India's largest private lender fast-tracks succession search as Jagdishan declines reappointment, ending a turbulent chapter marked by boardroom friction and a 27% share price decline.
body:
• Sashidhar Jagdishan will retire as HDFC Bank CEO on October 26, 2026, after declining to seek a third term despite the board's persuasion.
  • Deputy Managing Director Kaizad Bharucha is the leading internal candidate for the top job, with the bank also required by RBI rules to submit an external name.
  • HDFC Bank shares have fallen 27% in 2026, with the decline accelerating after former chairman Atanu Chakraborty's abrupt resignation in March over governance concerns.
  • Jagdishan leaves behind a mixed legacy: the successful completion of India's largest-ever corporate merger alongside boardroom friction, regulatory penalties, and investor frustration.

Sashidhar Jagdishan, the chief executive of HDFC Bank, will step down when his second term expires on October 26, ending a nearly three-decade career at India's largest private lender. The bank said Saturday that Jagdishan had "reiterated his decision to not seek reappointment" despite the board's efforts to persuade him to stay.

The departure caps a turbulent six months for HDFC Bank. Its shares have dropped 27% this year — roughly 40% of which are held by foreign investors — as a succession of leadership controversies eroded confidence in the institution that Aditya Puri built into a banking powerhouse.

A Tenure Defined by the Mega-Merger

Jagdishan, 61, joined HDFC Bank in 1996 as a finance manager, rose to chief financial officer in 2008, and succeeded founding CEO Puri in October 2020. His signature achievement was steering the 2023 merger of HDFC Ltd with HDFC Bank — one of the largest corporate amalgamations in Indian history — which dramatically expanded the bank's asset book.

The financial results under his watch were solid. Profit after tax grew from ₹31,117 crore in FY21 to ₹74,670 crore in FY26, with return on assets at 1.8% and return on equity at 14%. The bank projects FY27 profit of ₹84,230 crore.

"The board deeply appreciated his commitment, leadership, contribution to the growth and stability of the Bank and his role in the successful completion of one of the largest mergers in corporate India."

— HDFC Bank regulatory filing

But investors have voiced concern that the merger's promised benefits — particularly on net interest margins and deposit growth — have been slow to materialize.

Boardroom Friction and Governance Questions

The seeds of Jagdishan's exit were sown earlier this year. In March, non-executive chairman Atanu Chakraborty resigned abruptly, stating that practices at the bank were at odds with his "personal values and ethics." An external legal review concluded in June found no evidence to substantiate the governance issues Chakraborty raised, but the damage to investor sentiment was done.

Then in July, the board penalized Jagdishan and three other executives after determining that employees had engaged in "business overreach" while setting deposit rates for the Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation, a state agency. The extra payments to MSRDC were reportedly classified as marketing expenses in the bank's books.

Jagdishan had earlier indicated interest in a third term. But following the compounding controversies, Macquarie analysts warned that the outcome of his tenure would determine whether leadership concerns continued to weigh on the stock.

Succession Race Begins

The board has pledged to fast-track the appointment of Jagdishan's successor, aiming to complete the process ahead of the October 26 deadline. Under Reserve Bank of India rules, banks must submit multiple candidates for the CEO position for regulatory approval.

Deputy Managing Director Kaizad Bharucha has emerged as the leading internal candidate, according to Reuters, citing people familiar with the matter. Bharucha, who oversees the retail and wholesale businesses, is not due to retire until 2029 and meets RBI eligibility requirements.

The bank is simultaneously searching for an external candidate. The identity and credentials of the next CEO will be closely watched by investors hoping the transition can restore confidence in the bank's governance.

What It Means for NRI Banking

For the Indian diaspora, HDFC Bank is a critical financial partner — one of the most widely used banks for NRI accounts, remittances, and cross-border banking services. A smooth leadership transition will be essential to maintaining the trust of its large international customer base and the foreign institutional investors who hold a significant portion of the bank's equity.
